source: National Curriculum / statutory RSHE guidance (Relationships Education, Relationships and Sex Education, Health Education); PSHE Association programme of study themes and KS3 mental health lessons (Drive PSHE folder); TGA RSHE Policy 2026-27, Careers Education and Guidance Policy and Tarbiyyah Compass Character Framework 2026-27 (Drive); existing TGA PSHE Y5 lesson style. lessons.unit: Unit 1: Relationships and the online world
lessons.title: Belonging and friendship: healthy and unhealthy relationships
objectives: Describe the features of a healthy friendship
Recognise signs of an unhealthy or controlling relationship
Use respectful strategies to build and repair friendships, including online

keywords.def: a limit that shows what you are comfortable with
treating others as valuable and listening to them
understanding how someone else feels
people of a similar age you spend time with
good manners and character

starter: Bismillah. Name three qualities of a good friend.
What is the difference between a disagreement and bullying?
Give one example of a trusted adult.

teach.heading: What makes a relationship healthy?
teach.note: Say bismillah. Welcome pupils to Key Stage 3 PSHE and set ground rules. Ask pupils to list the people they have relationships with: family, friends, classmates, teachers, online groups. Draw out features of healthy relationships. Link to the hadith that none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself (Bukhari and Muslim). Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass values of Integrity and Excellence (adab). Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Warning signs of unhealthy relationships
bullets: Controlling who you see or talk to
Pressure to do things you do not want
Making you feel guilty or afraid
teach.note: Present invented examples: a friend checks your phone and gets angry about who you message; a group laughs at someone and says it is ‘just banter’. Ask pupils to rate each example: healthy, worrying or unsafe. Teach that unhealthy relationships are not always obvious at first. Emphasise that pupils are never to blame and that they can ask for support at any time.

teach.heading: Boundaries and respect
bullets: Boundaries are personal and different for everyone
You can say no, and so can others
teach.note: Practise assertive phrases: ‘I'd rather not.’ ‘That makes me uncomfortable.’ ‘Please stop.’ Teach that respecting another person's no is part of adab. Give examples about borrowing belongings, sharing secrets, sharing photos and personal space. Misconception: if someone does not say no loudly, it is fine to continue. Teach that we should stop when someone seems unsure.

teach.heading: Making and keeping friends in an online school
bullets: Be kind in chats and on camera
Keep group chats welcoming and inclusive
Ask an adult if a friendship worries you
teach.note: TGA pupils meet online, so friendship needs extra effort. Discuss netiquette: respond kindly, do not leave people out of group tasks, do not take screenshots to mock others, and follow the Behaviour and Online Conduct Policy. Ask: ‘What can you do this week to welcome someone new?’ Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Excellence.

teach.heading: Choosing good company
bullets: Choose friends who help you do good
Hadith: a person follows the way of his close friend
Repair friendships with honesty and apology
teach.note: Cite plainly: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said that a person is on the way of his close friend, so let each of you look at whom he takes as a friend (Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi). Discuss: ‘How can friends make us better?’ Teach a repair sequence: calm down, say sorry for your part, listen, agree what will change. Link to forgiveness.

practice: Sort into healthy, worrying or unsafe: (a) a friend shares your homework tips (b) a friend tells you not to talk to anyone else (c) a friend always borrows things without asking.
Write one assertive sentence you could use to refuse something you are uncomfortable with.
List two ways to make a new classmate feel welcome in an online lesson.
independent: Write a short scenario showing a warning sign in a friendship and how the person responds.
Create a ‘Friendship charter’ with five promises for your class.
Write a paragraph explaining how choosing good company supports Eeman and Integrity.
exit: Name two features of a healthy relationship.
Give one warning sign of an unhealthy relationship.
lessons.homework: Write down three qualities you bring to a friendship and one way you can improve as a friend.
lessons.send: SEND: use scenario cards with traffic-light sorting. EAL: provide key phrase cards for assertive responses. Stretch: research how the Prophet (peace be upon him) treated his companions and link three examples to friendship qualities.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Relationships and the online world
lessons.title: Social media, gaming and your digital footprint
objectives: Explain how to protect privacy and reputation online
Describe risks of group chats, gaming and social media and how to respond
Know how and where to report online concerns

keywords.def: the trail of information left by your online activity
a control that limits who sees your content
an image of what is on a screen, often shared
what other people think of you
to tell the platform or a trusted adult about a problem

starter: Bismillah. What is a digital footprint?
Give two examples of personal information to keep private.
What are the steps of Stop, Block, Tell?

teach.heading: Our online lives
bullets: We use apps, games and group chats
Most social media sets a minimum age of 13
teach.note: Say bismillah. Begin with a quick poll: which types of apps do pupils use? Do not ask for names of accounts. Explain that age limits are set by platforms and linked to data and safety rules. Ask: ‘What are the good things about being online?’ Then introduce the risks. Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Contentment: using technology in a balanced and grateful way. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Footprint and reputation
bullets: Posts, likes and comments can last
Others can copy, share and screenshot
Future schools and employers may look
teach.note: Explain that deleting does not always remove copies. Use an invented example: a joke message from Year 7 resurfaces in Year 11. Ask: ‘Would you be proud if your parents, teachers and a future employer saw this?’ Cite plainly: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said that whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should speak good or remain silent (Bukhari and Muslim). Apply it to typing.

teach.heading: Privacy and settings
bullets: Set accounts to private where possible
Accept only people you know in real life
teach.note: Walk through a mock privacy menu on screen. Teach the three-random-words password method and two-step verification. Explain that sharing passwords with friends, even trusted ones, can lead to hacked accounts and conflicts. Ask: ‘Why might an online friend not be who they say they are?’ Ensure pupils know that they should not meet online contacts.

teach.heading: Group chats and gaming
bullets: Never share photos of others without consent
Mute, block and leave if chat turns nasty
teach.note: Present an invented case: a group chat starts mocking a pupil's accent. Ask: ‘What are the options? What takes courage?’ Link to Qur'an 49:11 on not mocking others and 49:12 on avoiding backbiting. Mention that in-game purchases and loot boxes are designed to encourage spending, and that pupils should check with a parent before spending. Cyberbullying can be reported under the Anti-Bullying and Cyberbullying Policy.

teach.heading: How to report and get help
bullets: Block and report in the app
Save evidence, then tell a trusted adult
Report to the DSL at TGA
teach.note: Make sure all pupils know exactly who to tell at TGA. Explain that nobody will be punished for reporting in good faith. Introduce Report Remove, a tool from Childline and the Internet Watch Foundation that helps under-18s ask for nude or sexual images of themselves to be taken down. Keep this factual and brief; Y9 explores it further. Remind pupils that help is available without blame.

practice: Rewrite this post so it is kinder and safer: ‘Look where I am right now at Elmwood Park, come and find me!’
A friend sends you a screenshot mocking another pupil. List three possible responses and choose the best.
True or false? (a) Deleting a post always removes all copies. (b) Most social media platforms set a minimum age of 13. (c) You should accept any request from someone in your game.
independent: Create an infographic with five rules for a safe and positive digital footprint.
Role-play in pairs: one pupil is invited into a nasty group chat and the other helps them respond.
Write a letter to a friend explaining how to set up privacy settings and why.
exit: Give two reasons to be careful about what you post.
Name two places to report an online problem.
lessons.homework: Review the privacy settings on one account you use, with a parent or carer, and write three sentences on what you changed.
lessons.send: SEND: use a step-by-step visual checklist. EAL: pre-teach digital vocabulary with screenshots. Stretch: research the Online Safety Act 2023 and summarise how it protects children.

lessons.title: Naming feelings
lessons.bigQuestion: Is 'I feel bad' enough? How many different feelings could 'bad' hide?
objectives: To understand how naming our feelings accurately helps us manage them
successCriteria: All: name at least eight feelings, including mixed ones
Most: describe how a feeling shows in the body and in behaviour
Some: explain how naming a feeling helps us choose a healthy response
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: emotions as part of being human, guided by faith

keywords.def: a feeling such as joy, anger or fear
the words we use to name feelings precisely
something that sets off a feeling
what we choose to do about a feeling

hook.text: Is 'I feel bad' enough? How many different feelings could 'bad' hide?
hook.a: Many: disappointed, embarrassed, lonely, anxious, guilty, frustrated. Precise words help us respond.

islamicLink.text: Feelings are part of being human: the Prophet ﷺ wept when his son Ibrahim died and said the eye weeps and the heart grieves, but we say only what pleases our Lord (al-Bukhari). Islam guides what we do with feelings, not whether we have them.

starter.q: Which is a feeling word? A) Tuesday B) frustrated C) table
Name one thing that helps you feel calm.
starter.a: For example: a walk, du'a, talking to family.

starter.q: Who is a trusted adult at TGA?
starter.a: Form tutor, any teacher, the safeguarding lead.

starter.q: What is one healthy friendship quality?

teach.heading: A bigger feelings vocabulary
teach.note: A feelings wheel helps: core feeling in the middle, precise words outside.

teach.heading: Feelings in the body
teach.note: Noticing the body is an early warning.

teach.heading: Name it to manage it
teach.note: Model.

teach.heading: Model: from 'bad' to precise
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Your camera froze while presenting and others laughed.
steps: Notice: hot face, want to leave
Respond: breathe, rejoin, tell the teacher afterwards
model.answer: Embarrassed and hurt; breathe, rejoin, talk to the teacher

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Most precise word for 'I didn't get picked and I'm alone at break'?
check.why: Lonely names the feeling precisely; 'bad' and 'fine' hide it.

practice.q: Give a precise word: 'I worked hard but got a low mark.'
practice.model: Teacher thinks aloud: not angry at anyone; I hoped for more; so disappointed.

practice.q: Where might you feel anxiety in your body?

independent.q: Core: Feelings scenarios (pupil PDF): for six situations, name the precise feeling and one healthy response.
independent.a: Precise words and sensible responses for each.

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box, describe a mixed feeling you have had. Start: 'I felt both... and...'
independent.a: For example: I felt both excited and nervous on my first day at TGA.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why naming a feeling helps us control what we do.
independent.a: Naming slows us down and gives us a choice of response instead of reacting.

exit.q: Naming a feeling helps us... A) ignore it B) choose a healthy response C) blame others
Big question: what precise feelings could 'bad' hide? Name three.

lessons.homework: Keep a feelings journal for three days: one precise feeling word each day and what helped.
lessons.send: SEND: feelings wheel printed. EAL: feelings glossary with symbols. Stretch: research 'emotional granularity'.

Help list on the final slide: parents, form tutor, the school's designated safeguarding lead (contact in the portal), Childline 0800 1111

lessons.title: Strengths, goals and growth mindset
objectives: Identify personal strengths, interests and values
Set a SMART goal and break it into steps
Explain how a growth mindset and Islamic values support progress

keywords.def: something you are good at or a positive quality
specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound
believing that effort can improve ability
a hope or ambition for the future
doing everything to the best of your ability

starter: Bismillah. Name one thing you are good at.
What does ‘progress’ mean in the Tarbiyyah Compass?
Name one job that interests you.

teach.heading: Know your strengths
teach.note: Say bismillah. Ask pupils to think of strengths in four categories. Remind them that strengths can be academic, practical, creative, social and spiritual. Ask: ‘What would a friend say is your best quality?’ Allow pupils to pass. Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Contentment: being grateful for what Allah has given us. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Growth mindset
teach.note: Teach the word ‘yet’. Give examples: learning to type, memorising a surah, or learning a new maths skill. Cite plainly: Qur'an 53:39, that a human being will have only what they strive for. Misconception: talent alone decides success. Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass values of Resilience and Progress.

teach.heading: Setting SMART goals
teach.note: Worked example: vague goal ‘do better at Arabic’ becomes SMART goal ‘learn 10 new Arabic words each week for four weeks and test myself every Friday’. Ask pupils to improve a vague goal. Remind them to break big goals into small steps. Link to the hadith that the most beloved deeds to Allah are those done consistently, even if small (Bukhari and Muslim).

teach.heading: Ihsan: doing our best
bullets: Ihsan means excellence in all we do
Hadith: Allah has prescribed ihsan in everything
teach.note: Cite plainly: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said that Allah has prescribed ihsan, excellence, in all things (Muslim). Discuss what ihsan looks like in schoolwork, kindness and online behaviour. Ask: ‘How does having an intention to please Allah change how we work?’ Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Excellence.

teach.heading: Looking ahead
bullets: Many careers: health, technology, law, education
Subjects you enjoy lead to many paths
Talk to family and the careers lead
teach.note: Introduce the idea that careers are broad and change over time. Ask pupils to name jobs they know and group them into sectors. Mention that TGA has a Careers Education and Guidance Policy and a Careers Lead who will support them throughout their time at the school. Reassure pupils that they do not have to decide now.

practice: Turn this into a SMART goal: ‘I want to get better at reading.’
Rewrite as a growth mindset statement: ‘I am bad at maths.’
Name two of your strengths and one way to use them to help others.
independent: Write a personal strengths profile with three skills, three qualities and two interests.
Set one SMART goal for this half-term with three steps and a deadline.
Write a short paragraph on how ihsan could shape your goal.
exit: Give one example of a growth mindset sentence.
lessons.homework: Share your SMART goal with a family member and ask them to suggest one way to support it. Write what they said.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a SMART goal template with sentence starters. EAL: use a strengths word bank. Stretch: research a person who achieved a goal through persistence and describe the strategies used.

lessons.title: Growing up: puberty, bulugh and looking after yourself
lessons.bigQuestion: What changes when a child grows into an adult in Islam, and how do we look after ourselves?
objectives: Describe, in modest and factual terms, the main changes of puberty
Explain what bulugh (reaching maturity) means for a Muslim's duties
Describe the steps of ghusl and a good hygiene routine, and know who to ask for support
successCriteria: All: name three changes of puberty and one duty that begins at bulugh
Most: explain the signs of bulugh and when ghusl is required
Some: explain how Islamic teaching gives dignity and responsibility to growing up
lessons.crossCurricular: Islamic Studies: taharah and ghusl (Year 7 purification lesson); Science: cells, tissues and organ systems
lessons.smsc: Spiritual and moral: accountability before Allah (taklif), haya and dignity

keywords.def: the time when the body changes from a child's to an adult's
reaching maturity, after which a Muslim is responsible for their duties
a person who is accountable for carrying out Islamic duties
the full ritual washing of the whole body
chemical messengers in the body that cause the changes of puberty
modesty that protects a person's dignity and faith

starter: Bismillah. What does 'cleanliness is half of faith' teach us?
Name four parts of the body washed in wudu.
Give one healthy way to manage a worry.

teach.heading: Setting the scene
bullets: Taught to boys and girls separately
Parents have seen the lesson materials
Questions go to the anonymous question box
Growing up is part of how Allah created us
teach.note: Say bismillah. Teacher note: this lesson is taught to boys and girls separately, in line with the RSHE Policy, by a teacher of the same sex where possible. Parents are told in advance and can see all materials on the Parent Portal. Use correct, modest language and keep to what pupils need for health, hygiene and worship; use simple diagrams only. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Changes of puberty
bullets: Starts at different ages, usually between 8 and 14
Growth spurt, more sweat, oily skin and spots
Hair grows under the arms and on the body
Boys' voices deepen; girls begin their periods
teach.note: Explain that hormones cause puberty and that it starts at different times for different people; nobody is early or late in a bad way. Describe the changes plainly and briefly. With girls: a period (hayd) is a small monthly bleed from the womb that usually lasts a few days; explain how to manage it with pads, regular changing and good hygiene. With boys: wet dreams (ihtilam) are a normal sign of puberty and nothing to be ashamed of. Each group should know, in general terms, that the other also goes through changes, so that nobody is ever teased. Mood swings and stronger feelings are normal too.

teach.heading: Bulugh: becoming accountable
bullets: Hadith: the pen is lifted from a child until puberty
After bulugh, salah, fasting and covering are obligatory
Signs: a wet dream, periods for girls, or a set age
A new stage of responsibility, and of reward
teach.note: Cite plainly: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said that the pen is lifted from three: the sleeper until he wakes, the child until he reaches puberty, and the one who has lost his reason until he recovers (Abu Dawud; verify the wording before display). Bulugh (maturity) makes a person mukallaf: accountable for obligatory acts such as salah, fasting in Ramadan and the rules of covering ('awrah, and hijab for girls). Scholars name its signs: a wet dream for boys or girls, periods for girls, and, if no sign has appeared, reaching an age (15 lunar years in the view of most scholars). Pupils should ask a parent or a qualified scholar about details. Link to Qur'an 24:59: when children reach puberty they ask permission before entering rooms.

teach.heading: Ghusl and hygiene
bullets: Ghusl is needed after a wet dream and when a period ends
Wash daily, change clothes and use deodorant if needed

model.problem: Describe the Sunnah way of making ghusl.
steps: Make the intention in the heart and say bismillah
Wash the hands, then wash away any impurity
Pour water over the head three times, then wash the whole body, starting with the right side
model.answer: Ghusl is valid when, with the intention, water reaches the whole body; following the Prophet's way, as Aisha and Maymunah described it, is best.

teach.note: Teach the steps from the hadith of Aisha and of Maymunah (Bukhari and Muslim; verify the references before display). Rinsing the mouth and nose is part of the Prophet's way, and some scholars count it as required. With girls: prayers are not made up for the days of a period, but missed Ramadan fasts are made up later (Aisha's report in Muslim). Link to the Year 7 Islamic Studies lesson on purification.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which statement about bulugh is correct?
options: Islamic duties begin on a person's 18th birthday
After bulugh a Muslim is accountable for duties such as salah and fasting
Only adults over 18 need to make ghusl
check.why: Bulugh is maturity shown by its signs, after which a Muslim is mukallaf. Option A confuses it with the UK legal age of adulthood; C and D are wrong because the rules apply to girls and boys alike once they reach maturity.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. If many pupils choose A, explain the difference between bulugh in Islam and legal adulthood at 18 in the UK.

teach.heading: Feelings, haya and support
bullets: New feelings and mood changes are normal
Haya: lower the gaze and dress modestly
Talk to a parent first; teachers and your GP can help
Never tease anyone about how they are changing
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 24:30-31 tells believing men and women to lower their gaze and guard their modesty. Parents are the best first people to talk to; pupils can also speak to the pastoral team, the DSL or their GP. If a pupil seems worried or very distressed, follow safeguarding procedures. Close with a du'a for good health and purity of heart.

practice: True or false: (a) Puberty starts at the same age for everyone. (b) After bulugh, salah is obligatory. (c) Ghusl is valid only if water reaches the whole body.
Put the Sunnah steps of ghusl in order: make wudu; make the intention and say bismillah; pour water over the head and body; wash the hands.
Name two people you could ask for help with questions about growing up.
independent: Core: write a short guide, 'Growing up well', with three facts about puberty, two hygiene habits and the steps of ghusl.
Extend: explain in a paragraph what bulugh means and why it brings new responsibilities.
Stretch: explain how haya and taharah protect a Muslim's dignity, using one ayah and one hadith from the lesson.
exit: What must happen for ghusl to be valid?
Big question: what changes when a child grows into an adult in Islam?
lessons.homework: Talk with a parent or carer about growing up and ask them for one piece of advice about prayer or cleanliness. Write two sentences about what you learned.
lessons.send: SEND: simple labelled diagrams and a step card for ghusl; offer a quiet check-in. EAL: pre-teach puberty, bulugh and ghusl with images. Stretch: compare the age of bulugh in fiqh with the legal age of adulthood in the UK.

lessons.title: Managing worries and stress
lessons.bigQuestion: Is all stress bad? Can a little stress ever help?
objectives: To understand what stress is and how to manage it with healthy strategies
successCriteria: All: name three signs of stress
Most: choose a strategy for each kind of worry
Some: tell the difference between everyday stress and when to get help
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: the body's stress response (heart rate, breathing)

keywords.def: how the body and mind react to pressure
worry or fear that can feel strong
a planned way of coping
trusting Allah after doing our part (تَوَكُّل)

hook.text: Is all stress bad? Can a little stress ever help?
hook.a: A little can help us focus (before a test); too much for too long harms.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Allah does not burden a soul beyond that it can bear' (al-Baqarah 2:286) and 'Verily, with hardship comes ease' (ash-Sharh 94:5-6). Tawakkul means doing our part, then trusting Allah with the outcome.

starter.q: Most precise word for being left out?
Name one body sign of anxiety.
What are the steps: notice, name, ...?
Name a trusted adult.

teach.heading: What is stress?
teach.note: Good stress: a deadline helps focus. Too much: sleep and mood suffer.

teach.heading: Signs of too much stress
teach.note: Notice patterns, not one bad day.

teach.heading: Strategies
teach.note: Match strategies to worries.

head: Worry
Strategy
rows: List, break into steps, start with one
Calm down, talk honestly, ask an adult
Limit news, talk to family, make du'a

teach.heading: When to get help
bullets: It stops you sleeping, eating or learning
Thoughts of harming yourself: tell someone today
teach.note: Safeguarding: say clearly that you will always help and may need to pass worries on to keep them safe.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Best first step when homework feels overwhelming?
options: Break it into small steps and start one
check.why: Small steps make the task manageable.

practice.q: Do box breathing together for one minute.
practice.model: Teacher leads: in 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4.

practice.q: Choose a strategy for 'I'm worried about my first test'.
practice.a: Make a revision plan, sleep well, breathe, make du'a.

independent.q: Core: Make a personal stress plan (pupil PDF): my signs, three strategies, who I will talk to.
Extend: In the portal response box, explain how tawakkul helps with worry. Start: 'Tawakkul helps because...'
independent.a: Tawakkul helps because I do my part and then trust Allah with the result, so I worry less about what I cannot control.

exit.q: A little stress can... A) always harm B) help us focus C) never happen
Big question: when should stress make you ask for help?
exit.a: When it lasts, stops sleeping or learning, or you feel unsafe.

lessons.homework: Use one strategy from your plan this week and note whether it helped.
lessons.send: SEND: strategy cards. EAL: stress, worry, strategy. Stretch: research how exercise reduces stress hormones.

Help list on the final slide: parents, form tutor, the school's designated safeguarding lead (contact in the portal), Childline 0800 1111

lessons.title: Sleep, screens and healthy routines
lessons.bigQuestion: Teenagers often feel awake late at night. Is that laziness or biology?
objectives: To understand how sleep and screen habits affect health, mood and learning
successCriteria: All: state how much sleep teenagers need
Most: explain two ways screens can harm sleep
Some: design a realistic routine for an online learner and justify it
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: the circadian rhythm and melatonin

keywords.def: things we do regularly at set times
the body's 24-hour clock
habits that help good sleep
light from screens that can delay sleepiness

hook.text: Teenagers often feel awake late at night. Is that laziness or biology?
hook.a: Partly biology: the body clock shifts later in the teenage years, so routines matter more.

islamicLink.text: Allah says He made the night as a covering and sleep as rest (al-Furqan 25:47). The Prophet ﷺ disliked sleeping before Isha and talking after it (al-Bukhari). An early night helps us wake for Fajr.

starter.q: Name a sign of too much stress.
starter.a: Poor sleep, headaches, snapping at people.

starter.q: What is tawakkul?
starter.a: Trusting Allah after doing our part.

starter.q: Name a stress strategy.
starter.a: Break tasks into steps, breathe, talk.

starter.q: How many hours in a day?

teach.heading: How much sleep?
teach.note: NHS guidance for teenagers: about 8 to 10 hours.

teach.heading: Screens and sleep
bullets: Blue light delays the sleep hormone melatonin
teach.note: Devices out of the bedroom at night.

teach.heading: A healthy day for an online learner
bullets: Screens off an hour before bed
teach.note: Model.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: How much sleep do teenagers need?
check.why: NHS guidance for teenagers is about 8 to 10 hours.

practice.a: Same bedtime, screens off an hour before, dark cool room.
practice.model: Teacher lists three tips from their own routine.

independent.q: Core: Track yesterday: screen time, sleep, activity. Then plan a better day (pupil PDF).
independent.a: Honest record and an improved, realistic plan.

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box, persuade a friend to charge their phone outside the bedroom. Use two reasons.
independent.a: Blue light delays melatonin; notifications wake you; better sleep helps learning.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain how the teenage body clock and Fajr both affect bedtime choices.
independent.a: The body clock shifts later, but waking for Fajr means an earlier bedtime is needed for enough sleep.

exit.q: Blue light from screens can... A) help you sleep B) delay sleepiness C) do nothing
Big question: is feeling awake late laziness or biology?
exit.a: Partly biology (the body clock shifts), so good routines matter.

lessons.homework: Try your improved routine for five days and record bedtime and wake time.
lessons.send: SEND: routine planner with picture prompts. EAL: routine, habit, sleep. Stretch: research one study on screens and sleep.

lessons.title: Diet, exercise and healthy choices
lessons.bigQuestion: If a habit is unhealthy but feels good now, how do you choose what is better for later?
objectives: To understand how diet and physical activity affect long-term health and how to make realistic healthy choices
successCriteria: All: describe a balanced diet and the activity guideline
Most: evaluate a day's food and activity against the guidelines
Some: plan realistic changes and explain the long-term benefits
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: nutrition and the digestive system (Year 8 science)

keywords.def: foods from each group in the right amounts
any movement that raises the heart rate
sitting still for long periods
not too much, not too little

hook.text: If a habit is unhealthy but feels good now, how do you choose what is better for later?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Eat and drink, but do not waste by excess' (al-A'raf 7:31). The Prophet ﷺ said the strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, while there is good in both (Muslim). Looking after our bodies is part of our amanah.

starter.q: Teenagers need about how much sleep?
Name a sleep hygiene tip.
starter.a: Screens off an hour before bed.

starter.q: Name a food group.
starter.a: Fruit and vegetables, starchy, protein, dairy, oils.

starter.q: What does halal and tayyib mean?

teach.heading: A balanced diet
bullets: Fruit and vegetables: at least 5 a day
teach.note: NHS Eatwell Guide.

teach.heading: Activity
bullets: About 60 minutes a day on average
teach.note: UK CMO guidance for 5 to 18 year olds.

teach.heading: Evaluate a day
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Day: cereal, crisps and fizzy drink, pasta; 20 minutes walking; 7 hours on screens.
steps: Well: a starchy breakfast and dinner
Gaps: little fruit and veg, sugary drink, low activity
Change 1: swap fizzy drink for water
model.answer: Two realistic changes linked to the guidelines

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: How much activity should young people average a day?
check.why: The UK guideline is at least 60 minutes a day on average.

practice.q: Give one swap to cut sugar.
practice.a: Water instead of fizzy drink; fruit instead of sweets.
practice.model: Teacher shows a fizzy drink can label: about 35 g sugar per 330 ml can of regular cola; swap for water.

practice.q: Why is a long time sedentary harmful?
practice.a: Less fitness, weaker muscles and bones, poorer mood.

independent.q: Core: Evaluate your own typical day against the guidelines and plan two realistic changes (pupil PDF).
independent.a: Honest evaluation and two specific changes.
independent.model: Teacher evaluates the model day aloud.

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box, explain one long-term benefit of each change. Start: 'Over time...'
independent.a: For example: Over time, less sugar protects teeth and reduces the risk of type 2 diabetes.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain how fasting in Ramadan can be done healthily (suhur, water, balanced iftar).
independent.a: Eat a slow-release suhur, drink water between iftar and suhur, avoid overeating at iftar.

exit.q: Moderation means... A) never eating treats B) not too much, not too little C) only eating fruit
exit.a: B) not too much, not too little
options: Not too much, not too little

exit.q: Big question: how do you choose what is better for later?
exit.a: Think of long-term health, use small realistic changes, and remember our body is an amanah.

lessons.homework: Try your two changes for a week and record them.
lessons.send: SEND: food cards to sort. EAL: balanced, sedentary, moderation. Stretch: compare labels of two drinks.

lessons.title: Asking for help; trusted adults
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do people sometimes keep a problem to themselves even when it is getting worse?
objectives: To understand when and how to ask for help, and who can help us inside and outside school
successCriteria: All: name trusted adults at home and at TGA
Most: decide when a situation needs help and who to ask
Some: explain why safeguarding means some worries must be passed on
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: services that protect children (NHS, Childline)
lessons.smsc: Social: community care for one another

keywords.def: a grown-up who listens and keeps you safe
protecting children from harm
the staff member responsible for keeping pupils safe
kept private, unless someone is at risk of harm

hook.text: Why do people sometimes keep a problem to themselves even when it is getting worse?
hook.a: Embarrassment, fear of trouble, not wanting to worry others, or not knowing who to tell.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'The religion is sincere advice' (Muslim), and believers are like one body: when one part hurts, the rest responds (al-Bukhari and Muslim). Asking for help and helping others are part of our faith.

starter.q: UK activity guideline?
What is moderation?
starter.a: Not too much, not too little.

starter.q: Name a stress strategy.
starter.a: Break into steps, breathe, talk, du'a.

starter.q: How much sleep do teenagers need?

teach.heading: When to ask for help
bullets: A worry that will not go away
Feeling unsafe at home, school or online
teach.note: Never wait for it to 'get bad enough'.

teach.heading: Who can help
bullets: TGA: form tutor, any teacher, designated safeguarding lead
teach.note: Show where the safeguarding lead's contact is in the portal.

teach.heading: How to ask
bullets: Say: 'Can I talk to you about something?'
Message the teacher privately in Teams if speaking is hard
teach.note: Private chat to a teacher is fine; never share private worries in the class chat.

teach.heading: Safeguarding and confidentiality
bullets: If someone is at risk, adults must pass it on
That is to keep you safe, not to get you in trouble
teach.note: Be honest with pupils about this.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: A friend messages that someone online is asking for their photos. What should you do?
options: Tell a trusted adult straight away
check.why: This is a safeguarding risk; adults can act quickly to protect your friend.

practice.q: Who could you tell at TGA if something worried you?
practice.a: My form tutor, any teacher or the safeguarding lead.
practice.model: Teacher shows the portal page with the safeguarding lead's contact.

independent.q: Core: Scenarios sheet (pupil PDF): for five situations, decide whether to get help and who.
independent.a: Help sought from an appropriate adult for each risky situation.

independent.q: Extend: Make a personal help card: three people at home, two at TGA, one helpline.
Stretch: In the portal response box, explain why a teacher cannot always keep a secret. Start: 'A teacher must pass on...'
independent.a: A teacher must pass on a worry when a child may be at risk, so the right people can keep them safe.

exit.q: Childline's number is... A) 999 B) 0800 1111 C) 101
Big question: why do people keep problems to themselves, and what would you say to them?
exit.a: Fear or embarrassment; it is brave to tell, and adults can help.

lessons.homework: Put your help card somewhere you will see it, and tell a parent you have made it.
lessons.send: SEND: help card with symbols. EAL: help, safe, worry. Stretch: research what NHS 111 does.
